lines: Think about what a query engine actually does when you ask it for a Hive table. It doesn't open a ledger and read a committed version number.
It walks a folder tree and asks the file system, what's here right now? Whatever answer comes back, that's the table. This topic shows exactly where that habit breaks.
Picture someone running an insert. Before Hive can put that row anywhere, it needs to know which sub-folder it belongs in.
Who decides that folder — does the engine work it out from the data itself, or does a human just type it in and hope?
answer: The human types it in, and Hive takes their word for it. There's no cross-check against the row.
Type the date in the wrong format, or pull it from the wrong column, and nothing fails. You just get a quietly wrong answer later.

lines: This comes straight from Hive's own documentation, almost unchanged in decades. One table, two partition columns, and the storage layout is the column values themselves, folded into a file path.
There's no translation layer, no lookup — the path on disk and the partition key are the same string.
Here's the part that surprises people: Hive's catalog of tables doesn't watch the file system. It has no idea when a file shows up or disappears underneath it.
So the catalog and the disk can simply disagree, for as long as nobody runs the command that forces them back in sync.
Now imagine a write that needs to touch two of these folders at once — today's data and yesterday's correction, say.
If someone reads the table halfway through that write, do they see a consistent picture, or can they catch it between folders?
answer: They can absolutely catch it between folders. Before Hive had real transactions, a guarantee of atomicity never crossed a partition boundary.
Two folders in one logical write were always two separate, unrelated events as far as the storage was concerned.

lines: So this topic built that exact scenario and caught it happening. One folder finishes first, completely.
Then, right as the second folder is only halfway populated, a listing of the whole table is taken — and it comes back showing precisely that: one finished, one half done.
That isn't a contrived edge case either. It's the very reason Hive's own project added transactional support in the first place.
Tools streaming data in continuously were handing readers exactly this kind of half-finished view, and burying the file-tracking service under a mountain of tiny files besides.
There's a second cost hiding in all this, separate from correctness: just asking what files exist gets slower as there are more of them.
Time a real listing call at a small file count, then a much larger one, and the gap is obvious — and a full catalog resync pays that same tax, at table scale.
Step back and every one of these — the untrusted partition value, the catalog going stale, the missing atomicity, the slowing listing — comes from a single design decision.
Nobody ever wrote down what the table's state actually was. The table's state was defined as whatever a directory listing happened to say.
So here's the shape of the whole problem, pulled together. Partitions are just named folders, trusted without question.
A multi-folder write is never one atomic event. And listing gets more expensive the bigger the table gets. Every modern format exists to replace that listing with something explicit instead.
